769.s: He explains he learned left-handed and would have to switch the snare and tom-tom on another drummer's kit.
769.q: Well, it wouldn't be if one thing had to be changed, that would be the snare drum, unless they have, uh, a jungle drum alongside of them. I'd have to make the switch, you see, put the snare drum on this side and the jungle drum on the left-hand side.

769.s: Watkins does everything left-handed and kicks the bass drum with his left foot, which feels natural.
769.q: I'd have to take about six months practice to get accustomed to it, yeah.

769.t: Left-handed drummers: Snaggs Jones and Henry Martin
769.s: Russell asks about Snaggs Jones and other left-handed New Orleans drummers; Watkins says Henry Martin was left-handed and taught him to set up that way.
769.q: Did he use his left foot then too? Used his left foot too. That's practically where I got my learning from because he was learning me, you know, and he asked me what way I wanted to set up. So I set up left handed. And that's how I started out, playing left handed. I can't even right left handed. I…

769.s: Watkins explains his left-handed set-up, contrasts it with bop drummers' snare placement, and says he began left-handed as a child.
769.q: Well I don't know, not anything too much, but lots of people, it has them puzzled about how I play. They want to know how I'm set up. I say well I'm set up for a left hand style. They say well how do you do for, see I see some drummer look like they got that snare drum right in front of the bass…

769.t: No hi-hat and playing authentic jazz
769.s: George told him an authentic jazz drummer needs no hi-hat, and Watkins reflects that their records will keep their names alive.
769.q: He never did like them. No he never did like them. And I bought one and I tried and George told me, he said, George said, if you're going to stick to authentic jazz you don't need no hi-hat. He said, just your snare drum, bass drum, cymbal and your tum tum and wood block is all you need. I said,…

769.t: Brushes and a two-beat bass drum on the spirituals
769.s: He used wire brushes on the church-style record to keep volume under his vocals and the muted horns.
769.q: Never did. Never heard of a jazz band in my life being in the church. Yeah. Never heard of a jazz band in Oakland of the spiritual, felt like I was on a string. See? Yeah. But that actual wire brush and two beat on that, you never heard that before? No, no. That was just something I had this big...

769.t: Lewis's advice on a high stool, toe pedal technique and stamina
769.s: Lewis told him to use a high stool and rest his toes on the pedal; he describes the ankle action and long hours.
769.q: No, he didn't tell me about changing. He told me he wanted that authentic style of beating. Yeah. But the main thing was my seating arrangement.

769.t: Foot technique and avoiding the hi-hat
769.s: He started with his left foot, never used a hi-hat, plays from the hip and toes rather than the heel, and avoids ankle fatigue.
769.q: No, no, I'd have to practice about three or four months. Just to line that over. Yeah. Because see when I started, I started with my left foot.

957.t: How the snare drum is held and blown on while the bass drum keeps going
957.s: Allen presses for the mechanics: he stands, holds the snare drum to his mouth with the left hand, blows on the snare-side skin, and keeps beating with a stick and the bass drum.
957.q: They covered that from me. Yeah, they got that from you, huh? Yeah. But you hold your lips right up. I hold my lips right up.

957.t: Stick-on-stick technique learned from Mac Murray
957.s: Russell describes Foster's way of striking one stick with the other to change tone, which Foster says Mac Murray also did; they compare stick sizes.
957.q: That's right. You hit on both. That's to make the stick change tone. If you notice, you notice your sticks are almost making notes. Yeah, that's right. So you got to know how to squeeze them to a certain extent to make them change the tone. Yeah. Now, you watch. Your left stick, they always hit…

957.t: Keeping time: switching the beat between hand and foot
957.s: Foster demonstrates keeping four-four on the bass drum while the hand plays one-two, and switching between feet and hand in two-four time.
957.ch: Carey band, jazz and drum demonstrations
957.q: Well, anything you make it, your time, is how you figure it in your head. See, because I can take and make a one beat on the bass drum and still make a four-four beat with my hand. Okay. Or else I can make a one-two beat with my hand and still make a four-four beat on the bass drum. Uh-huh. It's…

957.t: Blowing and singing into the drum to imitate animals
957.s: Foster explains he sings and blows into the drum, imitating a lion, cow, pig or chicken in rhythm, for a chorus or two.
957.q: Well, most of the tone that imitates the song that we'll be playing. Well, I'd take it and I'd blow in the drum there and sometimes imitate a lion or cow, pig, or chicken, or something like that, duck, or anything like that. But it would be on the rhythm that the style that I would be playing on.

871.s: He works once or twice a week and sits low on a chair with a pillow.
871.q: Well, sometimes twice a week, sometimes once a week. Sometimes once a week, huh? It's been slow though, since Carnival's been slow. It's been slow since Carnival. You can work once a week nowadays, you're doing well. I'll tell you one thing. I see them drummers just about that high, and I can't sit…

871.t: Foot technique, parade drummer positions and marching left foot
871.s: He plays from the ankle; in the old days drummers marched at the back; marching starts on the left foot like rolls.
871.q: You leave your heel down on the floor and just from your ankle, your toe. Some fellas stomp the whole leg from the hip, you know. Well, I guess it's all how you start off. Yeah, I think they get more tired doing that than just your ankle. Yeah. I really, if I get tired, I really give a single beat…

871.t: Using the sock cymbal and single versus double beat
871.s: He praises the sock cymbal for keeping time and explains when to play single beat on the bass drum, as on Tiger Rag.
871.q: See. That keeps the time. See. That keeps the time with that. Yeah. That comes in on the after beat. Come on after beat. That's the time. Got you. You can't go nowhere. comes in on the after beat. Come on after beat. You can't go nowhere.

572.t: His time-keeping style and afterbeat hand
572.s: He keeps an afterbeat going on hi-hat and plays fills like an obligato behind soloists.
572.q: yeah well I never did I never would grab a cymbal and that and play on it all the time like that I used to have a a ring or whatever I had on my finger and I'd get a sizzle and I could run it underneath that get that sizzling sound that I'd get in that Swiss cymbal see I see

572.t: Why he never learned to read and his melodic drum style
572.s: He declined studio reading work, and describes his accented triplets and melodic approach versus modern drummers.
572.q: Yeah. The creative part was missing. That's why I didn't want to learn how to read music and learn how to play legitimate drums and then do all that. I could have probably worked in studios out there in California and said, uh, Big Boynton wanted me to play drums. He said, I'll show how to read all…

997.s: They discuss how drummers hold sticks, how fingers act as brakes, and that rolls are made from the wrist.
997.q: You see you have, you have, you have like a, like brakes. Like you're gonna, if you don't have brakes on these fingers, something has to stop these sticks. Yeah, that's right. They'll just shake out of your hand. That's right. What you call a bumper light. So you've got, excuse me, go ahead.…

997.t: Rudiments, practice pad, sticks and wrist exercises
997.s: He still practises on a pad made by a student, and talks about stick weights, ebony sticks and parade versus dance sticks.
997.q: not I didn't make it but a student of mine made it that gateway he made it nice solid one I had small one but he said I can make that so I say do you think he'd make one like that? sure in a few days he brought it down that's a nice solid one

402.t: Drummers Rod, Buck Rogers and Emmett Rogers; left-handed drumming
402.s: Talk of drummers who died, and of Monk and Emmett Rogers setting up and playing left-handed.
402.ch: Learning drums, WPA band and dance halls
402.q: Yeah, well Buck took my place. You see, this is recently. I compare it to the recent, at the famous door, see. There are two bands there. I remember Santa and the old man Christian. You know what I mean. It's a drum one place, see. I said, well, I didn't need anybody to call me up and all that. I…

862.t: Drum rolls, return tunes and march tempo
862.s: How drum rolls and bass drum beats signal the band, what tunes are played on return, and tempo.
862.q: You see, when the drummer roll, when the drummer roll, and the drummer beats all the time, it's a different thing. You see, when they're drumming the roll, they're fixing to play it. But now when they're marching, they just beat the march on it. But when they go to roll, like that, well, they're…

184.s: He uses medium-weight 7A sticks, plays brushes when needed, and makes a drag roll that can sound like wire brushes.
184.q: Some pieces I use them quite a bit, but I can put in there and do as much as my sticks. I can with brushes. I can play that song.

865.t: Twisting sticks and bouncing on the drum stool
865.s: He describes keeping the drum springs bouncing and twisting his sticks.
865.ch: Music as a way of life
865.q: I just keep them moving all the time. And I put a hand in with sticks in my hand, you know, twisting sticks. I just, my daughter, I tell him, I say, oh man, you're all the staff. I say, I like it because you walk in the middle. I say, you like something. I say, you like something.

49.t: Playing drums half and half; left-handed musicians
49.s: He explains his unusual right-footed, left-handed setup and they note left-handed players like Sharkey and Ray Lopez.
49.ch: Handedness and Gene Austin in California
49.q: I play half and half. I play right-footed and left-handed. See, I originally started all left. See? And then, I don't know, it was more, my right leg was better. I could keep better time with the right leg than I could with the left. And then you didn't, we didn't have those flying horse things…

829.t: Bass drum versus snare drum in parades; shrinking drum sizes
829.s: Robertson explains the bass drum comes in only when the snare cues it, that the snare works harder, and that the 22-inch bass drum replaced bigger, punishing ones.
829.q: No. Sometimes those fellas just do it, you know, say ordinary parades like that. The bass drum go along like that. But you don't have to. But that snare drum can't time all the time until it's time to play. Then the bass drum come in. But the bass drum, the fact of it, he don't work as hard as the…

634.t: Old-style snare, solos, cymbal choking and dynamics
634.s: Happy explains playing snare, block and rolls, drum solos, choking the cymbal, and band dynamics.
634.q: I'd play that block a while. And I'd play that a while and I'd switch to something else. And then when I'd take a drum solo, I'd give everything out. See, I'd work all my stuff.

8.t: Playing bass drum and cymbals in parades
8.s: Garland mostly played drums in parades and explains how he used cymbals with the bass drum, on and after the beat.
8.ch: New Orleans bands, brass bands and learning bass
8.q: I played drums. I played drums most of the time. Which one? I played bass drum. Yeah, I played good bass drum. I played it lately so I can't walk no more in a parade. I played bass drum.

571.t: How the music and the beat have changed
571.s: Lewis gives his view on how jazz has changed, repertoire, the beat in New Orleans, and the older drummers' overhead traps.
571.q: I would run a little bit of a winch. I would run a winch. I would truck a car and a big. It's not a one big car and it's a way to put it on the truck. It's balanced to catch an average in the middle. It's balanced to truck in all fields. I went to camped up on nothing but the Norwegian. I would…

192.t: Drumming as timekeeping and his cymbal style
192.s: He thinks of drums as timekeeping, favors snare, and describes his own light cymbal and Chinese block ideas.
192.q: Well, I think a drum, yeah. That's a part to you. I figured a drum is mostly a timekeeping instrument. It's strictly a time instrument, you know what I mean? And you just feel your own ideas, how they, you know, different numbers. You play, you understand the feeling. I think in the line of playing…

884.t: Drumming approach: steady beat, left foot, cymbal and press roll
884.s: The drummer's role is steady time; bass drum falls on the left foot in a march, cymbal half-beat, and his crushed roll done with the fingers.
884.q: Well, when I'm drumming like that, see what I do if a drummer like that, if you don't know, I'll try to talk to them, you know. And I'll take one stick, you know, like that, and try to show them when they hit. But some people come and try, they don't want to tell them nothing.

24.t: Fly drumming: Red Happy's style and Moore's multiple sticks
24.s: Moore explains foundation versus fly drummer, two-beat and four-beat playing, stick tricks, and how he uses four or even nine sticks and sits high.
24.q: Both. And his show, show drumming, some drumming, type of the, uh, in some numbers called for, what they call, beat two. I mean, two beat. That mean the foundation, to hold a band together. Mm-hmm. In some numbers he beat four. But he was good on both of them. Mm-hmm. He was what you call a…

832.t: Playing drums now; no drum lessons
832.s: Foster now plays drums, has been off sax for two years, and says he never had drum lessons.
832.q: I'm playing drums now, right now. In fact, uh, I've been off the sax now with Ciro, since we left the club at Tibidot. Yeah. And I've had two years, I've been off the sax. And New York, I was a failure job in Sweden, I've got to play rock and I've been doing a job, and I've played sax. Uh-huh.

306.t: Tuning snare and bass drums for the street and the dance band
306.s: Rene explains loosening the snare for the sun, a vibrating bass drum and tuning the bass drum to a key.
306.q: Yeah. I mean, this is sort of a bad, you know? As long as he's playing in time, you don't care how it sounds. But I think if a drum is tuned up real nice, it almost inhomens the band, you see? Most of them are sort of a tipply effect, you see? That gives them a nice sound. Because I know I used to…

504.t: Piano and drumming, tuning the drums
504.s: He says piano underlies his melodic drumming and he tunes drums by ear in melodic sequences.
504.ch: Time, Creative Music Studio and drumming
504.q: Oh they work great. Rhythmically it helps me when I’m playing piano. And the piano helps my drumming in terms of how to tune the drums, you know having fine tuning. Having maybe five or six notes that when you play, you play around the kit, you’re always playing melody. So you can make up melodies…

153.t: Big Sid Catlett and Jo Jones's lessons on hi-hat and brushes
153.s: Catlett taught him hi-hat and brushes at Atlantic City, and he tells of Jo Jones playing a newspaper and the wall at a New York club.
153.ch: Double bass drums and the great drummers
153.q: Fabulous. He was just the opposite of Chick Webb. He was enormous. He was a big man. When he played, the right stick looked like a toothpick in his hand. But yet he had the most finesse of anybody. A big guy – you expected him to have a blow like that metal drum stick I got in front, but, to quote…

471.t: Touch, brushes and the cymbal on So What
471.s: Cobb credits playing for singers with his touch, and recalls the cymbal crash on So What.
471.ch: Miles Davis band and Kind of Blue
471.q: That – I guess the sensitivity probably comes from having to work with singers, because you have to really be sensitive there. You have to listen, and you can’t overshadow. I got a lot of experience with Dinah Washington doing that. In fact, I had played with singers before I left Washington, but I…

237.t: Practice pad and Lovett's even hands
237.s: Lovett practises on a rubber pad and says he plays evenly with both hands.
237.q: Well you see Art, I'm an even-handed drummer. What I make with my right I make with my left and I can show you that.

98.s: He started with heavy sticks, now prefers lighter ones, plays an open roll, and says the secret is in the wrists.
98.ch: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
98.q: Yeah, I started out with heavier sticks, and I always compared a drummer with an athlete, with his feet and his legs and arms, muscles and all of this type of thing. As you grow older, you use a much lighter stick because you can't handle that heavy stick anymore, you know. Your wrist, your muscles…
